title: Best-First Search
body:
A family of search algorithms, not one algorithm. **Keep the frontier of unexpanded nodes in a
priority queue ordered by an evaluation function $f(n)$, and always expand the cheapest-looking
node next.** Change $f$ and you change which algorithm you have.

```
frontier ← priority queue containing the start node
loop:
    n ← pop the node with lowest f(n)
    if n is the goal: return the path
    expand n, push its children with their f values
```

The priority queue is a [[Heap]] in practice; see [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]].

## The family, by evaluation function

Two quantities do all the work. $g(n)$ is the cost of the path **already taken** to reach $n$, a
known number. $h(n)$ is a [[Heuristic]] estimate of the cost **remaining** from $n$ to a goal, a
guess.

| $f(n)$ | Algorithm | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| $g(n)$ | uniform-cost (Dijkstra's algorithm) | ignores the goal; provably optimal, explores everything cheap |
| $h(n)$ | **greedy best-first** | ignores the cost so far; fast, and **not optimal** |
| $g(n) + h(n)$ | **[[A* Search]]** | both; optimal when $h$ is admissible |

**Greedy best-first is the cautionary one.** Choosing purely by "which node looks closest to the
goal" is exactly the mistake of judging a route by how far the destination is as the crow flies:
it will happily walk into a dead end that pointed the right way, because nothing in $f$ remembers
what the trip has cost so far. It is fast and it will confidently return a bad path.

[[Dijkstra's Algorithm]] has the min-heap implementation and the non-negative-weights condition;
what matters here is that it is the $h = 0$ corner of this same table, and
[[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] owns the graph context around it.

## Informed against uninformed

Breadth-first, depth-first, and uniform-cost search are **uninformed**: they know the problem's
structure and nothing about where the goal is. Best-first search is **informed**, and the
information is entirely in $h$. That is the payoff and the risk: a good heuristic collapses the
search, a bad one is worse than useless because it has a cost and misleads.

Why bother, given the search space is finite: because it is finite the way a chess tree is finite.
See [[Game Trees]] for the $O(b^d)$ argument and [[NP-Complete]] for the reason no clever
algorithm makes the problem go away. **Heuristics are the response to intractability, and they buy
speed by giving up guarantees**, except in the one case [[A* Search]] covers.
